Every properly made boy reaches a time when he desperately wants to go digging for buried treasure. One day this desire suddenly seized Tom. He went looking for Joe Harper but could not find him. Next he tried Ben Rogers, who had gone fishing. Soon he came across Huck Finn the Red-Handed. Huck would do. Tom took him somewhere private and explained his idea in confidence. Huck agreed. He was always ready for anything that promised fun and cost nothing, since he had far too much of the kind of time that is not money. “Where should we dig?” Huck asked.

“Oh, almost anywhere.”

“What, is it hidden everywhere?”

“Of course not. It's hidden in very particular places, Huck. Sometimes on islands, sometimes in rotten chests beneath the end of an old dead tree's branch, exactly where its shadow falls at midnight. But mostly under the floors of haunted houses.”

“Who hides it?”

“Robbers, obviously. Who did you think? Sunday-school superintendents?”

“I don't know. If I had money, I wouldn't hide it. I'd spend it and enjoy myself.”

“So would I. But robbers don't do that. They always hide it and leave it there.”

“Don't they ever come back for it?”

“No. They mean to, but usually they forget the landmarks, or they die. Anyway, it stays there a long time, getting rusty. Then someone finds an old yellow paper explaining how to find the landmarks. It takes about a week to work out, because it's mostly symbols and hieroglyphics.”

“Hiero—what?”

“Hieroglyphics. Pictures and things that don't seem to mean anything.”

“Have you got one of those papers, Tom?”

“No.”

“Then how will you find the landmarks?”

“I don't need landmarks. They always bury it under a haunted house, on an island, or under a dead tree with one branch sticking out. We've searched Jackson's Island a little, and we can try again sometime. There's the old haunted house up Still-House stream, and there are loads of trees with dead branches—loads of them.”

“Is there treasure under every one?”

“What a question! No!”

“Then how will you know which to try?”

“Try them all!”

“But Tom, that'll take all summer.”

“So what? Suppose you find a brass pot containing a hundred dollars, all rusty and grey, or a rotten chest full of diamonds. How about that?”

Huck's eyes lit up.

“That's wonderful. Plenty good enough for me. Just give me the hundred dollars, and I won't need any diamonds.”

When Tom woke that morning, he could not remember where he was. He sat up, rubbed his eyes, and looked around. Then he understood. Dawn was cool and grey, and the deep stillness of the woods held a delicious feeling of rest and peace. Not a leaf moved; no sound interrupted Nature's vast meditation. Drops of dew beaded the grass and leaves. White ash covered the fire, and a slender blue breath of smoke rose straight into the air. Joe and Huck were still asleep.

Far off among the trees, a bird called. Another answered, and soon a woodpecker began to hammer. Slowly the cool, dim grey of morning brightened; just as slowly, sounds increased and life began to stir. As the boy watched thoughtfully, the wonder of Nature waking and setting to work unfolded before him. A little green worm crawled across a wet leaf, occasionally raising two-thirds of its body into the air to “sniff around” before moving on. It was measuring, Tom decided. When it began to approach him of its own accord, he sat perfectly motionless. His hopes rose whenever it came closer and sank whenever it seemed likely to turn away. At last, after a painfully long moment of consideration with its body curved in the air, it settled firmly on Tom's leg and started crawling over him. His heart filled with joy. This meant he would get a new suit of clothes—and without a doubt it would be a splendidly showy pirate's uniform. Now a line of ants emerged from nowhere in particular and went about their work. One struggled bravely past, clutching a dead spider five times its own size, and hauled it straight up a tree trunk. A brown, spotted ladybug climbed to the dizzying height of a blade of grass. Tom leaned close and said, “Ladybug, ladybug, fly away home. Your house is on fire, your children's alone.” She spread her wings and flew off to investigate. This did not surprise him: he had long known how readily this insect believed reports of fires, and he had taken advantage of her innocence several times before. Next came a dung beetle, stoutly pushing its ball along. Tom touched it to watch it fold its legs against its body and pretend to be dead. By now the birds were making an uproar. A catbird, that northern mimic, landed in a tree above Tom and joyfully sang her imitations of the neighbours. Then a shrieking jay swooped down like a flash of blue fire, landing on a twig almost within reach. It tilted its head and studied the strangers with intense curiosity. A grey squirrel and a larger fox squirrel came scampering along, pausing now and then to sit upright, inspect the boys, and chatter at them. These wild creatures had probably never seen a human being before and hardly knew whether they should be afraid.

“But when I saw that someone else loved you, when I imagined that you might be loved as something other than a sacred image of beauty and goodness, or that you might love another more passionately than you loved me, a demon woke inside me. I sent your lover away, and from that moment I have had no peace. I tried in vain to sleep or rest. My eyes would not close, and my blood was always in turmoil. I entered a new life like someone who dies full of hope and wakes in Hell. I will not stain your thoughts by describing my struggles, my rage against myself, or my despair. Let the unimaginable feelings of a guilty father remain hidden. The secrets of a heart in such agony must not become common talk. Everything within me was confusion, wickedness, remorse, and hatred, yet still the most tender love. What first made me firmly resolve to overcome my passion and give my child her father back was the sight of your deep, sympathetic sorrow. That brought me here. I thought that if I could revive my grief for your mother, along with the memories of her that had slept for seventeen years, all love for her child would die. In a moment of heroism, I decided to come alone: to leave you, the heart of my life, and not see you again until I could do so without guilt. But I could not manage it. I had overestimated my strength or underestimated my love. I would certainly have died if you had not hurried to me. If only my life had truly ended!

“And now, Mathilda, I must make my final confession. I was terribly mistaken to imagine I could overcome my love for you. I never can. Seeing this house, these fields and woods where my first love lived, seems only to have increased it. In my madness, I dared to tell myself that Diana died to give you life, that her spirit passed into your body, and that you should be another Diana to me. Each time I try to throw off this love, it clings more tightly. This guilty love is more unnatural than hatred. It ruins your hopes and destroys me forever.

“It would have been better to love despair, and safer to kiss her.

“No distance or passing time can tear from my soul what has become part of it. Since arriving here, I have not once stopped feeling this hell of passion, planted inside me to burn until everything is cold, stiff, and dead.
